extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in culture, society, and political authority (Victorian-era public and cultural critics)
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-philosophical essay analyzing English society's classes and arguing for culture (the 'best self' or 'right reason') as the legitimate basis of authority and standards in art, religion, and the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority based on the 'best self' (right reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority should be founded on our 'best self' — the impersonal, humane faculty of right reason developed by culture — rather than on the ordinary, class-instinctive self or mere class power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State should be the organ of the collective best self; citizens may provisionally strengthen the executive to preserve order when anarchy threatens, but only insofar as that authority is understood to represent right reason and not merely one class imposing its will. Anti-pattern: accepting authority that simply affirms the ordinary self of whatever class holds power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishop Wilson's two rules as moral guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Firstly, never go against the best light you have; secondly, take care that your light be not darkness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two maxims are offered as practical guidance: one must act according to one's best available conscience but also critically examine whether that 'light' is genuine reason or mere darkness. Arnold observes English emphasis on the first rule but negligence of the second; thus one should both follow conscience and ensure the conscience is informed (i.e., not mere prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture defined as the study of perfection (sweetness and light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is the study and development of perfection — by reading, observing, and thinking — which develops our best self and yields 'sweetness and light'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture is necessary to produce the 'light' that legitimates authority and to create standards of excellence. Anti-pattern: dismissing culture as impractical or fit only 'for a professor of belles lettres' (flouting culture), thereby leaving society dependent on ordinary selves and class-instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an authoritative centre and a scale of value in taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Without an authoritative centre (an organ of reason) and a recognized scale of aesthetic and intellectual value, public taste remains untrained and susceptible to the 'taste of the bathos' (low, trivial taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: literary and critical judgments should be ranked relative to nearness to an ideal centre of correct information, taste, and intelligence (example: Saturday Review as nearer such a centre than the British Banner). Anti-pattern: treating all organs of opinion as equally authoritative and failing to cultivate a scale of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge doctrines or movements by followers or force
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a following or the presence of arms ('200,000 souls; an army of 20,000 rifles') does not make a doctrine true or important; popularity and force are not proper tests of intellectual or moral worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply stricter tests to doctrines (truth, reason, moral quality) rather than counting adherents or military strength. Example/anti-pattern: Mr. Hepworth Dixon's account of the Mormons, which regards numbers and rifles as evidence of seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose unnecessary demonstrations that risk tumult when orderly change is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When great changes (a 'revolution by due course of law') are necessary, order is also necessary; therefore unnecessary multitudinous processions, meetings, and demonstrations that risk tumult should be discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One's best self 'enjoins us to set our faces against' such demonstrations and to support executive measures that prohibit them in the interest of establishing the State as the organ of right reason. Caveat: this support is justified only insofar as it advances the State as the collective best self and not merely the dominance of a particular class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic (Barbarians) standard: exterior culture, courage, and potential defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracies (Barbarians) possess exterior culture — politeness, accomplishments, prowess, chivalry — and virtues like high spirit and self-confidence; their virtuous mean (e.g., Lord Elcho) shows politeness and courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect: an aristocratic insufficiency of inward 'light' (thought and feeling) — culture tends to be chiefly exterior; ideal improvement requires a deeper inward cultivation (more 'soul' beneath good looks and manners). Anti-pattern: allowing worldly splendour and pleasure to seduce one from pursuing genuine intellectual/perfective culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-class (Philistines) standard: self-reliance and industrial achievement, with defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-class (Philistines) have achieved great works via self-reliance, business, and industrial prowess; their virtuous mean is exemplified by figures like Mr. Bazley, while excesses show in figures like the Rev. W. Cattle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect: a helpless inaptitude for the great works of the middle-class in some individuals and an overarching self-satisfaction that resists self-transformation; anti-patterns include preferring machinery of business, chapels, tea-meetings, and narrow utilitarian comforts over pursuit of 'sweetness and light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Working-class (Populace) standard: sympathy and action, with excesses and defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The working-class can possess 'bright powers of sympathy and ready powers of action' (the virtuous mean exemplified by Mr. Odger), but excesses (e.g., Mr. Bradlaugh) can manifest as iconoclasm and intemperate talk that risks social danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect (in some older or undeveloped portions): dulled sympathy and impaired capacity for large-scale collective action (e.g., the 'Needy Knife-grinder' or the poacher overindulged in gin). Anti-patterns: intemperance in talk leading to social disorder; untrained action easily running away with the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and cultivation of individuals bent on perfection across classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Within every class there are 'aliens'—natures bent on pursuing perfection (culture) who transcend class-instincts and develop the best self; they are the true carriers of 'sweetness and light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should recognize and nurture these persons because their extrication of the best self helps check unchecked class-life and promotes humane ends. Practical note: the number of such persons depends on innate bent and external encouragement or hindrance.
